newsitem.title: HUNGARY: DATA ON HUNGARY 1956 SHOWS KRUSCHEV LOATHE TO INVADE.
newsitem.headline: DATA ON HUNGARY 1956 SHOWS KRUSCHEV LOATHE TO INVADE.

text.p: New Russian and Chinese data on the 1956 Hungarian Uprising unveiled at a conference in Budapest on Friday shows how close Soviet leader Nikita Kruschev was to recognising Hungary's revolutionary government of the time.

Documents recently released by Russian president Boris Yeltsin show that two days before the final Soviet invasion to overthrow the government of Imre Nagy, Kruschev was still exploring ways of recognising Nagy's leadership and pulling all Red Army troops out of Hungary.

The evidence appears as Hungarians prepare to mark the 40th anniversary next month of the uprising against Stalinism which was suppressed by the Soviet tanks after 12 days. Around 25,000 people are estimated to have died in the fighting, which many scholars see as signalling the deathknell of communism.

Vitaly Afiani, deputy director of the former archives of the Soviet Communist Party central committee, said the documents consist mainly of notes taken by Vladimir Malin, head of the chancellery of the Soviet Communist Party central committee, of unminuted Soviet politburo meetings.
The sessions were held between the outbreak of the uprising on October 23 and the Soviet invasion beginning on November 2.

"The Malin notes show (politburo) sessions were held continuously on the Hungarian question in an agitated way," Afiani told Reuters. "The majority of the presidium were in favour of the Nagy government and even discussed the possibility of the withdrawal of troops."

According to Afiani, Kruschev saw Nagy, a reform Communist, as someone who would work within the Communist system. He was also influenced by the Suez crisis following Egyptian president Gamal Abdul Nasser's nationalisation of the Suez Canal.
Britain and France were preparing to invade Egypt to take the canal back and Kruschev did not want the Soviet Union to be accused of similar "imperialistic" behaviour.

However, Afiani's evidence shows how the picture had dramatically changed by the morning of October 31st following the British and French invasion of Egypt and crucial consultations the night before with the Chinese delegation, which included current Chinese leader Den Xiao Ping.

"Kruschev opened the morning session by saying the presidium had to fundamentally revise the condition it took the day before," Afiani said. "He expressed the view that if troops pull out of Hungary that would 'cheer up the imperialists', the British, French and the Americans."

Jian Chen, who left communist China in the 1980s to become a leading Cold War scholar in the United States, on Friday presented new evidence from Deng's interpreter in Moscow and the then Chinese leader Mao Zedong's political secretary.
"We already knew China pushed the Soviet Union to take a harsh attitude," Chen told Reuters. "Now we see the contrast with their attitude to Poland, where they warned against Moscow's intervention."
Kruschev had allowed Poland to replace its Stalinist government with a reform communist leadership but was now considering invading the country to end reforms, a move which China opposed.

However, Chen said reports of communist party members being lynched in Budapest and the general tone of international reporting as communicated to Peking by the Chinese Embassy in Budapest led Mao to conclude the Hungarians were anti-communist rather than just anti-Soviet as the Poles were.
"On the evening of October 30th Deng and Chinese party vice chairman Liu Shaoqi, told Kruschev 'You have to do something, you cannot give up Hungary.'"
The pressure on Kruschev was increased by reports of the invasion of Egypt, which Kruschev probably then thought would fall to the West, with Hungary possibly following, Afiani said.
In fact the United States intervened soon afterwards to force the British and French to withdraw their forces.
